title: KALANYOS AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
summary:
In the case of Kalanyos and Others v. Romania, the applicants—Sandor Kalanyos, Tamas Kalanyos, and Istvan Rozsa—are Romanian nationals of Roma origin living in the hamlet of Plăieşii de Sus, Harghita County. Their case highlights the acute vulnerability of Roma communities to violent collective reprisals and the failure of state protection. The events began on 6 June 1991, when a fight broke out between four Roma men, including the first applicant, and a nightwatchman. Following this, non-Roma villagers launched a revenge attack, fatally injuring one Roma man and seriously harming another. On 8 June, a public notice threatened the burning of Roma homes, prompting the Roma, including the applicants, to seek police protection. Instead of intervening, local authorities advised the Roma to flee. On 9 June 1991, non-Roma villagers cut off electricity and communications before setting fire to all twenty-seven Roma houses in the settlement, leaving the applicants and their families homeless and forced to live in stables under dire conditions for a year.

Despite clear evidence and witness statements, the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation, ultimately closing the case without identifying or prosecuting the perpetrators. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 6 (right to a fair trial), 8 (right to respect for private and family life), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination). The case was declared admissible, but the judgment focused on the admissibility rather than a finding of violation at this stage.

This case is significant as it exposes the persistent pattern of anti-Roma violence and impunity in post-communist Europe, underscoring the urgent need for effective state protection and accountability for crimes targeting Roma and Traveller communities.
